explain.say: The keys are wired in a grid of rows and columns. A small chip in the keyboard checks the grid hundreds of times a second and spots which crossing has closed, so it knows exactly which key you pressed.

explain.say: The keyboard sends a number called a scan code, not a letter, to the computer. The operating system translates it using your keyboard layout, so the same key can type a different letter in France.

faq.q: What happens under a keyboard key?
faq.a: Each key presses a switch. In a membrane keyboard, a rubber dome squashes two printed plastic layers together; in a mechanical keyboard, each key has its own metal-contact switch with a spring.
asks: How does a keyboard key work?

faq.a: Instead of a wire for every key, keys sit where row and column wires cross. The keyboard chip powers one row at a time and checks which column answers, which tells it the key. It also ignores the tiny flickers as contacts bounce, called debouncing.
asks: How does the keyboard chip find the key?

faq.a: A scan code is a number that identifies a physical key, such as the key in the top-left letter position. The keyboard sends codes when a key goes down and comes up, so the computer also knows when you hold a key.
asks: What does a keyboard send to the computer?

faq.q: How does the computer know which letter I typed?
faq.a: The operating system looks up the scan code in your keyboard layout. On an English layout the top-left letter key types Q; on a French AZERTY layout the same key types A. Shift and other keys change the result too.
asks: Why do keyboards in other countries type different letters?

faq.q: How fast does a key press appear on screen?
faq.a: Usually within a few hundredths of a second. The keyboard is checked every few milliseconds, the computer processes the letter almost instantly, and the screen shows it on its next refresh, about every 17 milliseconds at 60 hertz.
asks: Why is there a delay when I type?

facts: USB keyboards are commonly polled 125 times a second by default, and gaming keyboards up to 1,000 times a second.
On a French AZERTY keyboard, the key where English QWERTY keyboards have Q types A.
